title: Nail-Down vs Glue-Down vs Floating Hardwood: Which Installation Method Is Right?
meta: Nail-down over plywood, glue-down over concrete, floating for click-lock engineered: how Wills Flooring picks the method in Lynnwood homes at $3.25 per sq ft.
keywords: nail down vs glue down hardwood, floating vs glue down engineered hardwood, hardwood installation methods, nail down hardwood over plywood, glue down hardwood on concrete, hardwood installation Lynnwood WA
offers: Hardwood floor installation, engineered or solid

blocks.lead: Nail-down is the right method for solid or engineered hardwood over a plywood subfloor, which covers the main and upper levels of nearly every Lynnwood rambler and split-level. Glue-down is the answer over a concrete slab or where you want the most solid feel. Floating is for click-lock engineered over slab, radiant heat or a sound underlayment.
blocks.detail: Wills Flooring's installation labor is $3.25 per sq ft for engineered or solid regardless of method. What changes between methods is the material line: nails, adhesive, moisture barrier or underlayment, quoted at the free estimate.

blocks.html: The method question usually comes up at our showroom on 196th St SW when someone from Alderwood or Martha Lake has read three forum threads and gotten three answers. The confusion is fair: online advice comes from every climate and every kind of house. In Lynnwood the answer is unusually clear, because most of our housing stock is 1960s to 1980s ramblers and split-levels with one plywood level and, in many split-levels, one slab level. Each level gets a different method, and here is why.

items.title: Nail-down (and staple-down)
items.text: Boards are fastened through the tongue into a wooden subfloor with cleats or staples every 6 to 8 in. It is fast, quiet underfoot, and lets solid wood expand and contract naturally. It requires at least 3/4 in plywood or 23/32 in OSB with joists at 16 in. It cannot be used over concrete or over radiant tubing.

items.tag: For slabs and the solidest feel
items.title: Glue-down
items.text: Boards are set into a trowelled bed of urethane adhesive over concrete or plywood. Done well it is the most solid, quiet floor of the three, with no hollow sound. It needs a flat, dry, tested slab, a moisture-blocking adhesive or separate barrier, and 24 hours before heavy traffic. Solid wood over 5 in wide is rarely glued; engineered is ideal.

items.title: Floating
items.text: Engineered planks click or glue to each other at the edges and rest on a foam or cork underlayment, attached to nothing. It goes over slab, radiant heat, old vinyl and slightly imperfect subfloors, and it is the easiest to meet condo sound rules with. The trade-off is a slightly hollower feel and sound, and a need for expansion gaps and transitions in large rooms.

blocks.text: Glue-down or floating over a slab?

a.title: Glue when
items: You want the most solid, quiet floor with no hollow footfall
The slab is flat within 3/16 in over 10 ft, or you are willing to level it
Wide-plank engineered, where floating floors can flex at the joints
The floor is permanent and you are not planning to change it in ten years

b.title: Float when
items: A sound underlayment is required by the HOA
The slab has minor unevenness you would rather not grind
Radiant heat or old vinyl is under the new floor
Budget is tight: no adhesive cost and a faster install

blocks.title: Never skip the moisture test on a Lynnwood slab:
blocks.text: Lower levels of split-levels built in the 1960s and 1970s often have no vapor barrier under the concrete, and Snohomish County groundwater rises all winter. We test slab moisture before quoting a glue-down or floating install. If readings are high, the fix is a moisture-blocking adhesive or a proper vapor retarder under a floating floor, not hope.
Method mistakes we get called to fix

items.html: Nailing into a subfloor that is too thin. Some 1960s houses have 1/2 in plywood or old plank subfloor. Cleats do not hold, boards squeak within a year. A layer of 3/8 in plywood first solves it.
Gluing over a dusty or sealed slab. Adhesive bonds to whatever is on top: dust, old paint, curing compound. Grinding or scarifying the slab is not optional.

Floating a big open room without expansion. A 30 ft run of floating engineered needs its gap at every wall and, past the manufacturer's limit, a transition. Trap it under cabinets or an island and it buckles.
Floating the stairs. Stair treads are always fastened, both glued and nailed, whatever the field of the floor is. A loose tread is a fall waiting to happen.

Not asking which method is in the quote. Our hardwood installation quotes name the method for each level and list adhesive or underlayment on its own line, so you know exactly what is going under your floor.

faq.q: Is glue-down or nail-down hardwood better?
faq.a: Neither is better everywhere; the subfloor decides. Over plywood or OSB, nail-down is faster, proven and lets solid wood move naturally. Over concrete, nail-down is impossible and glue-down gives the most solid result. Many Lynnwood split-levels use nail-down upstairs and glue-down on the slab below with the same plank.

faq.q: Does the installation method change the price?
faq.a: Wills Flooring's labor is $3.25 per sq ft for engineered or solid hardwood with any method, and $2.75 for unfinished. The difference shows on the material line: urethane adhesive and moisture barrier for glue-down, underlayment for floating, cleats for nail-down. Slab leveling, if needed, is also quoted separately at the estimate.

No. Solid wood expands and contracts too much across its width to hold together as a floating panel; the joints would open and the floor would drift. Solid hardwood is nailed over a wood subfloor or, in narrow widths, glued. If you want a floating floor, choose a click-lock or edge-glued engineered product.

faq.q: Does a floating floor feel cheap or hollow?
faq.a: It can if it is installed over a thin foam pad on an uneven subfloor. Over a quality dense underlayment on a flat surface, a thick engineered floating floor feels close to glue-down. Some hollowness at footfall is inherent, which is why we recommend glue-down where the slab is flat and the budget allows.

faq.q: Can I glue hardwood directly to a concrete slab in a Lynnwood basement?
faq.a: Yes, engineered hardwood can be glued to a below-grade or on-grade slab after a moisture test shows acceptable readings and the surface is ground clean and flat. We use a moisture-blocking urethane adhesive. If moisture is high, a floating floor over a vapor retarder is the safer choice, or vinyl plank for the wettest spaces.

faq.q: Which method is best for radiant floor heat?
faq.a: Floating engineered hardwood is the most common and forgiving choice over radiant systems, followed by glue-down with a radiant-rated adhesive. Nail-down is used only with systems designed for it, since a cleat through a tube is a serious repair. Keep engineered wear layers moderate and let the system run before and after installation.
